_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II: Sohrab overthrows Rustam; the refused elixir; the lament. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: Sohrab Throws Rustam and Spares Him on a False Custom
title.zh: 蘇赫拉布摔倒父親卻因「規矩」放生

region.zh: 兩軍之間的戰場（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 18-20

summary.en: In their first wrestling the champions part fordone, the sire in anguish and the son exhausted; the youth mocks the old man's weakness. On the second day Sohrab, who in his own words perceives in him the marks whereof his mother spake and presages that he must be Rustam, nonetheless grapples him, up-leaping with a lion's spring, and hurls the great hero to the ground, sitting on his breast with a bright steel dagger to cut off his head. Rustam cries out that the customs and laws of arms with us are not as yours: none may take a foeman's head the first time his back is on the ground — a rule invented on the spot. Suhrab, partly through confidence, partly through fate, and no doubt through magnanimity, lets his father go and chases an antelope.
summary.zh: 首日角力，父子皆力竭——父悲痛、子力盡；少年譏老者氣衰。翌日蘇赫拉布自言「在他身上看見母親所述的印記，心中預感必是魯斯塔姆」，仍以獅躍之勢抓住其腰帶，將偉大的父親摔在地上，跨坐其胸拔出匕首欲取首級。魯斯塔姆急呼：「我方兵法規矩與你們不同——第一次將對手摔倒者不得斬首！」此規乃臨場杜撰。少年因自信、因天命、亦因寬宏，放走了父親，轉身追逐羚羊。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Cross-ref: the slaying itself is the existing record rustem-sohrab (Atkinson translation). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Suhrab, still musing on his mother's words, went spear in hand. They chose a battle-ground where room was scant and fought with javelins till points and whipping broke; then, wheeling leftward, closed with their Indian scimitars, and showered sparks from their blades; then took their massive maces and fought on until their weapons bent beneath the blows. The chargers staggered and their bards dropped off; both were fordone and hand and arm both failed, with bodies running sweat, with mouths dust-choked, and tongues thirst-cracked, at length the champions parted, the sire in anguish and the son exhausted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 18 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Love stirred in neither of these twain, no trace of wisdom was there, love showed not its face! The fish in streams, wild asses on the plain, and beasts of burden know their young again, but toil and lust forbid a man to know the difference between a child and foe. Then Rustam thought: I never yet beheld a Crocodile fight thus; compared with this to fight the White Div was an easy task; to-day my heart despaireth through a man!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 18 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suhrab had addressed Human: that lion-man who striveth with me is as tall as I am and hath a dauntless heart; he favoureth me in shoulder, breast, and arm, and thou wouldst say that some skilled workman laid us out by line. His very feet and stirrups move my love and make me blush, for I perceive in him the marks whereof my mother spake. Moreover my heart presageth that he must be Rustam; I may not challenge my sire or lightly meet him in the combat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They wrestled like two lions until their bodies ran with sweat and blood. From sunrise till the shadows grew they strove until Suhrab, that maddened Elephant, reached out, up-leaping with a lion's spring, caught Rustam's girdle, tugged amain, and, shouting with rage and vengeance, hurled him to the ground; raised him aloft and, having dashed him down, sat on his breast with visage, hand, and mouth besmirched with dust, then drew a bright steel dagger to cut off Rustam's head. The customs and laws of arms with us are not as yours, cried Rustam: in wrestling none may take a foeman's head the first time that his back is on the ground; but having thrown him twice and won the name of Lion then he may behead the foe. The brave youth hearkened to the old man's words, in part through confidence, in part through fate, in part no doubt through magnanimity; Suhrab let Rustam go, turned toward the plain, pursued an antelope that crossed his path, and utterly forgot his recent foe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

region.zh: 卡烏斯營帳（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab sec. 22

summary.en: Rustam sends Gudarz to the Shah for the elixir in his treasury which hath the power to make the wounded whole: if thou at all art mindful of my deeds, let thy heart feel for me in my distress. Kaus honours Rustam exceedingly, yet reasons: if I send the elixir, Sohrab will live, will strengthen Rustam's back, and doubtlessly bring ruin on myself — didst thou not hear him say he would behead a thousand in Iran and hang Kais alive upon the gibbet? To cherish foes is to invite contempt. The evil nature of the Shah, Gudarz reports to Rustam, is like a colocynth in constant fruit.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆遣古達爾茲向王求取「能醫百傷」的庫藏靈藥：「念我一生功勞，可憐我此番苦痛。」卡烏斯敬重魯斯塔姆，卻盤算：若賜藥，蘇赫拉布必活，將助魯斯塔姆之背，必危及我身——你沒聽他說過要斬千人、吊死卡烏斯嗎？「養虎遺患。」古達爾茲回報：王之刻薄如常結苦果的苦葫蘆。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Kaus' refusal seals the tragedy. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Then to Gudarz said Rustam: famous hero of ardent soul, bear for me to Kaus a message, tell him what hath chanced, and say thus: with a dagger have I pierced the reins of my brave son; may Rustam's life be short. If thou at all art mindful of my deeds let thy heart feel for me in my distress. If thou hast in thy treasury a drug which hath the power to make the wounded whole, send somewhat graciously to me forthwith, together with a cup of wine. My son, by thy good fortune, may recover yet, and stand like me a slave before thy throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah said: who hath lustre in my sight exceeding that of elephantine Rustam? I do not wish him ill but honour him exceedingly, yet, if I send the elixir, Sohrab, an elephantine chief, will live, will strengthen Rustam's back, and doubtlessly bring ruin on myself. Thou hast heard the language of Sohrab: I will behead a thousand in Iran and hang Kaus alive upon the gibbet. If he surviveth great and small will quake; to cherish foes is to invite contempt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereat Gudarz returned like smoke to Rustam and said: the evil nature of the Shah is like a colocynth in constant fruit; he hath no equal in the world for harshness, and never helpeth any one in trouble. Go unto him in person, be thy part to bring the light to his benighted heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Rustam Mourns Sohrab and Blames Hajir
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆哭子而咎海吉爾

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. II, Suhrab secs. 21-25

summary.en: Sohrab, dying, begs that the Turkman host be let depart unscathed, and names Hajir, the evil-purposed stirrer up of strife, who withheld the news of his father. Rustam, broken, seeks the Shah's elixir, is refused, and carries the dying boy toward the palace; one overtakes him with the news that Sohrab hath passed from this wide world. He removes his helm and scatters dust upon his head: hath this that hath befallen me — to slay my son in mine old age — befallen another? Then he seizes Hajir by the throat, and would behead him, but the nobles save the traitor from death's door.
summary.zh: 臨終的蘇赫拉布懇求放突厥大軍全身而退，並道出隱匿其父消息的「興風作浪的海吉爾」。魯斯塔姆求藥不得，抬著垂死之子走向王帳；途中有人來報：蘇赫拉布已離人世。英雄摘盔撒土於首：「白髮之年親手殺子——天下有誰遭此慘事？」隨後扼住海吉爾咽喉欲斬之，眾貴族方救下那叛徒。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: While clamour raged Sohrab said thus to Rustam: the Turkmans' case is altered since my day is done. Use all thine influence that the Shah may not attack them; they approached Iran through trust in me, and I encouraged them. How could I tell, O famous paladin, that I should perish by my father's hand? Let them depart unscathed, and treat them kindly. I marked in thee the tokens that my mother described but trusted not mine eyes. The stars decreed that I should perish by thy hand; I came like lightning and like wind I go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 21 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zawara came forthwith and gave the message, and he, the warrior that taught Sohrab the art of war, thus answered: 'twas Hajir, that evil-purposed stirrer up of strife, who hid the matter of your general, and when Sohrab sought token of his sire spake not but left his mind in ignorance. The black behaviour of Hajir hath brought this ill on us. Then Rustam hurried to his wounded son with Tus, Gudarz, and Gustaham, and seizing a dagger to behead himself was held back by the chieftains weeping their own hearts' blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 21-22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Rustam called for an embroidered robe and, having laid the youth thereon, set off; but as he went one overtook him, saying: Sohrab hath passed from this wide world, and asketh no more a palace of thee but a bier. The father started, sighed, and groaning closed his eyes, then lighting swift as wind removed his helm and scattered dust upon his head, while all the great men also wept and wailed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: O warrior-youth exalted and a paladin by birth! the sun and moon, the breastplate and the helm, the crown and throne, will never see thy peer, he cried in mournful tones. Hath this that hath befallen me, to slay my son in mine old age, befallen another? The hero was distracted at the words of Human about Hajir; he quitted the battlefield and coming to Hajir laid hold upon his throat and threw him down, then drawing forth a dagger of bright steel was minded to behead him, but the nobles took part with him and saved him from death's door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Suhrab secs. 23, 21 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
